q: 1. Reduce level of line of collimation is 50 m, staff reading at the base of pillar in 1.15 m then find the reduce level of base of pillar
explain: RL of point = RL of Collimation (HI) - Staff Reading = 50 - 1.15 = 48.85 m.

q: 2. Reciprocal leveling eliminates
explain: Reciprocal levelling, as noted earlier, eliminates both the combined curvature/refraction error and the collimation error, since observations are taken from instrument positions near each end point.

q: 3. The Bench Mark of a point is 400m. Back sight reading at bench mark is 2.20 and fore sight reading of point A is 2.10 then find the RL of the point A
4. Which of the following statement is correct?
options: In levelling, the effect of curvature is to decrease the staff reading.
The effect of refraction in levelling is to increase the staff reading.
The combined effect of curvature and refraction in levelling is to increase the staff reading.
explain: Actually curvature increases the apparent staff reading (makes points look lower), refraction (partially) decreases it, but per the answer key given, the combined net effect statement along with the other individual statements is taken as correct overall, hence option (d), all of the above, is marked correct in this text.

q: 5. In the double application of principle of reversion, the apparent error is
explain: When the principle of reversion is applied twice (doubled), the apparent error observed becomes four times the actual true error in the instrument's adjustment.

q: 6. Find the RL of collimation line if the RL of BM is 100 m & BS staff reading is 5.35 m
explain: The Reduced Level of the collimation line is simply the Height of Instrument (HI), which is RL + BS = 100 + 5.35 = 105.35 m.

q: 7. Levelling deals with measurements in
explain: Levelling essentially measures vertical differences of elevation between points, but these are determined with reference to a horizontal line of sight, so it involves both horizontal and vertical planes.

q: 8. The elevation (BM) of point A is 100 m. Back sight reading at A is 20 and fore sight reading at B is 30 m. Find the RL of point B
9. In levelling, the correction for curvature (in meters) is equal to
explain: The standard formula for the curvature correction, with D in kilometres, is Cc = 0.0785*D2 metres.

q: 10. A level line is
options: line parallel to the mean spheriodal surface of earth
line passing through the centers of cross hairs and the center of eye piece
line passing through the objective lens and the eye piece of a dumpy or tilting level
explain: A level line is a curved line that remains parallel to the mean spheroidal (geoid) surface of the earth at every point, distinguishing it from a straight horizontal line.

q: 11. Tilting levels are used for
explain: Tilting levels are designed for high precision because the line of sight can be adjusted slightly for each reading to be perfectly horizontal.

q: 12. In levelling, the correction for combined curvature and refraction (in meters) is equal to
explain: Accounting for the effect of atmospheric refraction (about 1/7th of the curvature effect, in the opposite sense), the combined correction reduces to 0.0673*D2 metres, with D in kilometres.

q: 13. The following sights are taken on the turning point
explain: At a turning (change) point, both a fore sight (to close the previous instrument setup) and a back sight (to begin the next instrument setup) are taken.

q: 14. The adjustment of horizontal cross hair is required particularly when the instrument is used for
explain: Correct adjustment of the horizontal cross hair is important across multiple uses of the instrument - leveling, prolonging straight lines, and measuring horizontal angles - so all of these apply.

q: 15. Compensator is used to make the line of sight perpendicular to vertical axis in case of
explain: An automatic level contains a compensator (an optical pendulum) that automatically levels the line of sight even if the telescope is slightly tilted.

q: 16. Pick up the odd instrument
explain: A dummy level is used for levelling (vertical measurement), whereas the prismatic compass, theodolite, and box sextant are all instruments primarily used for measuring horizontal angles/directions, making the dummy level the odd one out.

q: 17. In leveling across a hill, the level should be set up on
explain: When leveling up or down a slope, the instrument is placed on the side of the hill in a 'zigzag' pattern to maintain a manageable staff height.

q: 18. An angle between the inclined line of sight and the horizontal is called
explain: The angle measured between an inclined line of sight and the horizontal plane is, by definition, the vertical angle.

q: 19. Level surface is parallel to
explain: A level surface is a curved surface that is at all points normal to the direction of gravity. It is not parallel to a flat horizontal surface.

q: 20. The surface perpendicular to the direction of the gravity is
explain: By definition, a level surface (like the mean surface of a still lake) is always perpendicular to the local plumb line (direction of gravity).

q: 21. The sensitiveness of a level tube decreases if
options: radius of curvature of its inner surface is increased
diameter of the tube is increased
length of the vapor bubble is increased
both viscosity and surface tension are increased
explain: Sensitivity of the level tube decreases when both the viscosity and surface tension of the enclosed liquid are increased, since the bubble then moves more sluggishly in response to tilt.

q: 22. The Philadelphia rod is a type of
explain: The Philadelphia rod is a two-section telescopic leveling staff that can be extended for higher readings.

q: 23. A 'level line' is a
options: line parallel to the mean spheroidal surface of earth
line passing through the center of cross hairs and the center of eye piece
line passing through the objective lens and the eyepiece of a dumpy or tilting level
explain: A level line follows the curved level surface of the earth, and is therefore best described as a line parallel to (following) the mean spheroidal surface of the earth, not a straight horizontal line.

q: 24. In a constant level tube, size of the bubble remains constant because upper wall is
explain: In a constant-bubble level tube, the upper wall has a relatively larger radius of curvature compared to the main curved surface, which keeps the bubble length constant despite temperature changes.

q: 25. The correction for curvature as applied to staff reading is
explain: Curvature correction ($C_c$) is always subtractive from the staff reading because the earth curves away from the horizontal line. Formula: $-d^2/2R$.

q: 26. The curvature and refraction corrections applied to staff readings respectively are
explain: Curvature correction is negative (subtractive) while refraction correction is positive (additive) to the staff reading.

q: 27. If the level tube is out of adjustment by an angle e, when the telescope is rotated through 180°, it becomes
explain: Rotating the telescope by 180° doubles the angular error relative to the vertical axis, hence 2e.

q: 28. Line of collimation is
options: is the same line of sight
the line joining point of intersection of cross hairs and optical centre of object glass
the geometrical axis of the telescope
the line parallel to the bubble tube axis
explain: The line of collimation is the specific line of sight defined by the cross-hair intersection and the optical center of the objective lens.

q: 29. Pick up the odd statement
options: temporary adjustment of Dumpy level are to be performed at every set up
the eye piece need not be adjusted after the first set up when the same surveyor is taking readings
parallax error is completely eliminated when there is no change in the staff reading when the eye is moved up and down
focus the objective towards a white or bright background for the clear visibility of cross hairs
explain: Option (d) is odd because you focus the *eyepiece* (not the objective) against a white background to see the cross-hairs clearly.

q: 30. "Cross-sectioning" and "Longitudinal sectioning" is
options: when less number of intermediate sight exist
explain: Profile leveling involves taking readings along a center line (longitudinal) and at right angles to it (cross-sectioning) to map the terrain.

q: 31. An invert is taken when the point is
options: above the line of the sight
explain: An 'inverted staff' reading is taken when the point (like the underside of a bridge or ceiling) is higher than the instrument's line of sight.

q: 32. Ten readings were recorded in a level field book. If the instrument was shifted after 2nd and 6th readings, then the fore sight are
explain: The reading taken immediately before a shift is a Fore Sight. Additionally, the final reading of any run is always a Fore Sight. Thus: 2nd, 6th, and 10th.

q: 33. A staff reading taken on a bench mark or a point known elevation is called
explain: A staff reading taken specifically on a bench mark or point of known elevation, used to determine the height of instrument, is called a back sight reading.

q: 34. Fifteen readings were recorded in a level field book. If the instrument was shifted after 5th, 10th and 15th readings, then the fore sights are
explain: Similar to the previous logic, shift readings and the final reading are Fore Sights: 5th, 10th, and 15th.

q: 35. A staff reading taken on a point whose elevation is to be determined as on a change point called
explain: A staff reading taken on a point whose elevation is to be determined (typically the last reading before shifting the instrument, at a change point) is called a fore sight reading.

q: 36. In profile levelling, staff readings on two neighboring pegs 20 m apart are 1.20 and 1.00 respectively. Therefore, the proposed road had a
explain: Difference in level = 1.20 - 1.00 = 0.20 m (rise). Gradient = Rise/Distance = 0.20/20 = 1/100. Since the reading decreased, the ground rose.

q: 37. In profile leveling, staff readings on two neighboring pegs 20 m apart are 1.00 and 1.20 respectively. Therefore, the proposed road has a
explain: The difference in level is 1.20 - 1.00 = 0.20 m over a distance of 20 m. The gradient is 0.20/20 = 1/100. Since the reading increased from 1.00 to 1.20, the ground is lower at the second point, indicating a falling gradient.

q: 38. The following readings were taken on a uniformly sloping ground, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 1.2, 1.7, 2.7. Hence the difference in level between the first and last station is
explain: The difference in level is calculated by the sum of Back Sights minus the sum of Fore Sights. Here, the change in reading sequence (2.0 to 1.2) indicates a change point. (0.5 + 1.2) - (2.0 + 2.7) = 1.7 - 4.7 = -3.00, which represents a 3.00 m fall.

q: 39. The following readings were taken on a uniformly sloping ground, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0. Hence the difference in level between the first and last station is
explain: For a continuous slope without change points, the difference is simply the last reading minus the first reading: 3.0 - 0.5 = 2.50 m fall.

q: 40. The points A and B are 1530 m apart across a wide river... The true difference in level between A and B would be
explain: Using the reciprocal leveling formula: True Difference = [(B1 - A1) + (B2 - A2)] / 2. Based on the table: [(3.810 - 2.165) + (2.355 - 0.91)] / 2 = [1.645 + 1.445] / 2 = 1.545 m.

q: 41. During levelling staff readings are taken 1.0, 0.8 & 0.6 from consecutive horizontal cross hairs, the staff intercept should be
explain: The staff intercept is the difference between the top and bottom hair readings: 1.0 - 0.6 = 0.4.

q: 42. In survey it was recorded that Σfall = 0 then
explain: If there are no 'falls' recorded in the leveling book, it implies every subsequent point was higher than the previous one, meaning the ground is continuously rising.

q: 43. In a survey it was recorded that Σrise = 0, then
explain: If there are no 'rises' recorded, every subsequent point must be lower than the previous one, indicating the ground is continuously falling.

q: 44. The bench mark of a station A is 300 m and back sight reading at the point A is 2 m & fore sight reading of station B is 3 m. Find the RL of station B
explain: Height of Instrument (HI) = RL + BS = 300 + 2 = 302 m. RL of B = HI - FS = 302 - 3 = 299 m.

q: 45. The RL of bench mark is 100.0 m and back sight reading at the bench mark is 2.555 m find the staff reading of IS if RL of IS is 100.055 m
46. The image formed by the objective in the plane of cross hairs is
explain: The objective lens of a surveying telescope forms a real, inverted image of the object in the plane of the cross hairs, which is later magnified (and often re-inverted by additional optics) via the eyepiece.

q: 47. The brightness of the image ... the magnifying power
options: varies directly as the square of
varies inversely as the square of
explain: Image brightness varies inversely as the square of the magnifying power of the telescope; higher magnification spreads the same amount of light over a larger image area, reducing brightness.

q: 48. The following sights are taken on a 'turning point'
explain: A turning point (change point) requires both a foresight (to close the current instrument setup) and a subsequent backsight (from the new instrument position), so both are taken there.

q: 49. The ratio of the focal length of the objective to that of an eye-piece of a telescope is called its
explain: The magnification (magnifying power) of a telescope is defined as the ratio of the focal length of the objective lens to the focal length of the eyepiece.

q: 50. The rise and fall method
options: is less accurate than height of instrument method
is not suitable for leveling with tilting levels
provides a check on the reduction of intermediate point levels
quicker and less tedious for large number of intermediate sights
explain: The key advantage of the rise and fall method over the height of instrument method is that it provides a complete arithmetic check on the reduction of levels for every point, including intermediate sights.
